front_blocks.md: Define **antibody**.

back_blocks.md: An **antibody** is a **glycoprotein** (immunoglobulin) made by **plasma cells** that binds specifically to a particular **antigen**.

cards.front_md: Define **antibody**.
cards.back_md: An **antibody** is a **glycoprotein** (immunoglobulin) made by **plasma cells** that binds specifically to a particular **antigen**.

front_blocks.md: Describe the **structure** of an antibody.

back_blocks.md: An **antibody** is made of **four polypeptide chains** — two **heavy** and two **light** chains — held together by **disulfide bonds** in a **Y-shape**.
It has two **antigen-binding sites**.

cards.front_md: Describe the **structure** of an antibody.
cards.back_md:

front_blocks.md: What is the **variable region** of an antibody and why is it important?

back_blocks.md: The **variable region** has a specific shape that is **complementary** to one particular antigen, so each antibody binds to only **one** type of antigen.

cards.front_md: What is the **variable region** of an antibody and why is it important?

front_blocks.md: Define **antigen-antibody complex**.

back_blocks.md: An **antigen-antibody complex** is the structure formed when an **antibody** binds to its specific **antigen**.

front_blocks.md: How does having **two antigen-binding sites** relate to an antibody's function?

back_blocks.md: An antibody can bind **two pathogens** at once, clumping them together (**agglutination**) so that phagocytes can engulf them more easily.

front_blocks.md: What is the role of the **constant region** of an antibody?

back_blocks.md: The **constant region** allows the antibody to **bind to receptors** on phagocytes, helping them to recognise and engulf the pathogen.

front_blocks.md: Define **monoclonal antibody**.

back_blocks.md: **Antibodies** that are all **identical** because they are produced by **cloned cells** derived from a single B-lymphocyte, so they bind to one specific **antigen**.

front_blocks.md: Define **hybridoma**.

back_blocks.md: A cell made by **fusing** a **B-lymphocyte** with a **tumour (myeloma) cell**; it produces antibodies and can divide indefinitely.

cards.front_md: Define **hybridoma**.
cards.back_md: A cell made by **fusing** a **B-lymphocyte** with a **tumour (myeloma) cell**; it produces antibodies and can divide indefinitely.

front_blocks.md: Outline the **hybridoma method** for producing monoclonal antibodies.

back_blocks.md: An animal (e.g. a mouse) is **injected** with an antigen so it makes **B-lymphocytes** that produce the required antibody.
These B-lymphocytes are **fused** with **tumour (myeloma) cells** to form **hybridoma** cells.
Hybridomas making the required antibody are **selected** and **cultured**.
They **divide** to produce large amounts of identical **monoclonal antibodies**.

cards.front_md: Outline the **hybridoma method** for producing monoclonal antibodies.
cards.back_md:
An animal (e.g. a mouse) is **injected** with an antigen so it makes **B-lymphocytes** that produce the required antibody.

These B-lymphocytes are **fused** with **tumour (myeloma) cells** to form **hybridoma** cells.

Hybridomas making the required antibody are **selected** and **cultured**.

They **divide** to produce large amounts of identical **monoclonal antibodies**.

front_blocks.md: Why are B-lymphocytes fused with **tumour (myeloma) cells**?

back_blocks.md: B-lymphocytes do not divide well in culture, but tumour cells **divide rapidly and indefinitely**, so the hybridoma can both make antibody **and** keep dividing.

cards.front_md: Why are B-lymphocytes fused with **tumour (myeloma) cells**?

front_blocks.md: Why are the antibodies produced described as **monoclonal**?

back_blocks.md: They are all **identical** and specific to **one antigen**, because they are made by **clones** of a single hybridoma cell.

front_blocks.md: Outline the principle of using monoclonal antibodies in the **diagnosis** of disease.

back_blocks.md: A monoclonal antibody is made to **bind specifically** to an antigen linked to the disease.
Attaching a **marker** (e.g. a dye or radioactive label) then shows **whether** or **where** that antigen is present.

front_blocks.md: How can monoclonal antibodies be used to **locate** cancer cells or blood clots?

back_blocks.md: The antibodies are made to bind to **antigens** on the target cells and carry a **radioactive or fluorescent marker**, so the site can be **detected** by scanning.

front_blocks.md: Outline the principle of using monoclonal antibodies in the **treatment** of disease.

back_blocks.md: They are made to bind specifically to a target (e.g. antigens on **cancer cells**), so they can **block** its activity or **deliver a drug** directly to it.

front_blocks.md: What is a **"magic bullet"**?

back_blocks.md: A **monoclonal antibody** with a **drug or toxin attached** that delivers the drug only to **target cells** (e.g. cancer cells), reducing damage to healthy cells.

front_blocks.md: Why do monoclonal antibody treatments cause **fewer side effects** than some other treatments?

back_blocks.md: Because each antibody binds to only **one specific antigen**, they target **only** the diseased cells, so healthy cells are largely **unaffected**.

front_blocks.md: Define **active immunity**.

back_blocks.md: Immunity gained when the body's own immune system is **stimulated by an antigen** to make its **own antibodies** and **memory cells**.

front_blocks.md: Define **passive immunity**.

back_blocks.md: Immunity gained by receiving **antibodies** made by **another** organism; no memory cells are made, so it is **short-lived**.

cards.front_md: Define **passive immunity**.
cards.back_md: Immunity gained by receiving **antibodies** made by **another** organism; no memory cells are made, so it is **short-lived**.

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between **natural** and **artificial** immunity?

back_blocks.md: **Natural** immunity is gained through **normal life**, e.g. an infection or antibodies from the mother.
**Artificial** immunity is gained through **medical intervention**, e.g. vaccination or an injection of antibodies.

front_blocks.md: Give an example of **natural active** immunity.

back_blocks.md: Making your **own antibodies** and memory cells after **catching** and recovering from an infection.

front_blocks.md: Give an example of **artificial passive** immunity.

back_blocks.md: Being **injected with antibodies** made by another organism, e.g. anti-venom or tetanus antibodies.

front_blocks.md: Why is **passive** immunity short-lived while **active** immunity is long-lasting?

back_blocks.md: Passive immunity provides only ready-made antibodies and **no memory cells**, so it ends when they break down.
Active immunity produces **memory cells**, giving long-term protection.

front_blocks.md: Define **vaccine**.

back_blocks.md: A preparation containing **antigens** that stimulates the immune system to produce **antibodies** and **memory cells** without causing the disease.

cards.front_md: Define **vaccine**.
cards.back_md: A preparation containing **antigens** that stimulates the immune system to produce **antibodies** and **memory cells** without causing the disease.

front_blocks.md: How does a vaccine provide **long-term immunity**?

back_blocks.md: The vaccine's **antigens** stimulate a **primary immune response**, producing **antibodies** and **memory cells**.
If the real pathogen later enters, **memory cells** trigger a rapid **secondary response**, destroying it before symptoms develop.

front_blocks.md: What do vaccines contain?

back_blocks.md: **Antigens**, e.g. from a **weakened (attenuated)**, **dead**, or otherwise modified pathogen, or purified antigen molecules.

Vaccines contain live, fully active pathogens.

front_blocks.md: Define **herd immunity**.

back_blocks.md: When a **large proportion** of a population is **immune** (e.g. vaccinated), so the pathogen cannot spread easily, protecting even those who are **not immune**.

cards.front_md: Define **herd immunity**.
cards.back_md: When a **large proportion** of a population is **immune** (e.g. vaccinated), so the pathogen cannot spread easily, protecting even those who are **not immune**.

front_blocks.md: How do vaccination programmes control the spread of an infectious disease?

back_blocks.md: By making most of the population **immune**, there are **fewer people** who can catch and pass on the pathogen, so **transmission** is reduced and outbreaks are prevented (**herd immunity**).

cards.front_md: How do vaccination programmes control the spread of an infectious disease?
cards.back_md: By making most of the population **immune**, there are **fewer people** who can catch and pass on the pathogen, so **transmission** is reduced and outbreaks are prevented (**herd immunity**).

front_blocks.md: Why must a **high percentage** of the population be vaccinated for a programme to work?

back_blocks.md: So that too few **susceptible** individuals remain for the pathogen to spread between, breaking the **chain of transmission**.

back_blocks.md: The pathogen's **antigens change** (antigenic variation), so existing vaccines and memory cells no longer **recognise** it, e.g. influenza.

back_blocks.md: A **worldwide** vaccination programme made enough people immune that the virus could **no longer spread**, so smallpox was **eradicated**.
